sets.wrong: as an intensifier for something figurative
sets.why: Used as an intensifier it means its own opposite, and there is no other word that does its real job — which is to tell a reader that the surprising thing you just said is not a metaphor.

items.sentence: The retaining wall was ___ holding the hillside up.
He was ___ climbing the walls waiting for the decision.

gloss.unique: the only one of its kind

sets.wrong: unusual, distinctive — and so open to 'very', 'quite', 'rather'
sets.why: Either a thing is the only one or it is not; there are no degrees. 'Fairly unique' asks the word to be a synonym for unusual, which it already has several of.

items.sentence: The site is ___ in the city: no other lot fronts on all four streets.
It is a rather ___ approach to the corner.

sets.why: If you say you are nauseous you are describing your effect on other people. The sense has shifted far enough to be standard, but the older one is still the more precise.

items.sentence: A ___ smell came off the standing water.
She felt ___ after the third hour in the van.

gloss.dilemma: a choice between two options, both unwelcome

sets.why: The di- is two. If there is no fork, and no cost either way, it is a problem — which is a perfectly good word.

items.sentence: The ___ was stark: lose the trees or lose the affordable units.
The drainage ___ took months to sort out.

gloss.plethora: an unhealthy excess; more than is good

sets.why: It came from medicine, where it meant too much blood. A plethora is never a good thing; if you mean plenty, say plenty.

items.sentence: A ___ of overlapping guidelines has made the process unnavigable.
The park offers a ___ of things to do on a Saturday.

sets.why: A travesty of justice is a process that impersonated justice badly. It is about a bad copy, not about a bad outcome.

items.sentence: The consultation was a ___ of engagement: one meeting, unadvertised.
Losing the whole terrace to fire was a ___.

sets.why: The point is that nothing has happened to it yet. A scrubbed floor is clean; only an untouched one is pristine.

items.sentence: The wetland is one of the last ___ stretches on the escarpment.
The site office was ___ by the time the tour arrived.

gloss.effete: exhausted; no longer able to produce

sets.why: It described soil and animals that had stopped being fertile. The 'affected dandy' sense arrived by sound association and buried a useful word.

items.sentence: An ___ institution going through motions it no longer believes in.
He affected an ___ drawl that annoyed everyone.

gloss.inchoate: just begun; not yet fully formed

sets.why: It sounds like 'incoherent' and is not related. Inchoate says early, not disordered.

items.sentence: The plan was still ___ — a sketch and a list of intentions.
The meeting was ___, with four people talking at once.

gloss.cohort: a group sharing a characteristic, usually age or year

sets.why: It was a Roman unit and is now a statistical one. A cohort is a band of people, not one of them — 'he and his cohorts' makes each person a group.

items.sentence: That ___ entered the market just as prices peaked.
He arrived with two ___ from the development company.

gloss.parameter: a quantity that defines how a system behaves

sets.wrong: a boundary or limit — that is a perimeter
sets.why: Parameters are the dials, not the fence. 'Within the parameters of the study' usually means within its scope, which is a perimeter idea wearing the wrong word.

items.sentence: Changing one ___ shifts the whole forecast.
The fence marks the ___ of the works area.

gloss.epicentre: the point on the surface directly above where something originated

sets.wrong: the centre of the most intense activity
sets.why: The epi- means above. It is not the middle of the action; it is the spot on top of the source, and it is often not where the worst damage is.

items.sentence: The ___ was twelve kilometres north of the town, but the damage ran south.
The market was the ___ of the neighbourhood's life.

gloss.crescendo: a gradual increase in volume or intensity

sets.why: It is the getting louder, not the loud part. 'Rose to a crescendo' says it rose to a rise.

items.sentence: The objections built in a slow ___ over three meetings.
The argument reached its ___ just before the vote.

gloss.alibi: evidence that you were somewhere else

sets.why: It is Latin for 'elsewhere'. If it does not place you somewhere else, it is an excuse.

items.sentence: His ___ was solid: he was in Ottawa all week.
She offered the usual ___ about workload.

sets.why: It is always a complaint. Asking a colleague to check the verbiage in a clause tells them the clause is bloated.

items.sentence: Strip the ___ and the policy is two sentences long.
Please check the ___ of the second condition.

sets.why: A moot was an assembly for debate, and law students still moot cases. North American usage has flipped it to mean the argument is over — so the phrase now says opposite things on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and is worth avoiding when it matters.

items.sentence: Whether the easement survived the severance is a ___ point, and the lawyers disagree.
Once the appeal was withdrawn the question became ___.

gloss.ilk: the same kind, the same sort

sets.wrong: a disreputable sort — a slur by implication
sets.why: It is neutral: 'of that ilk' simply means of that kind. It has picked up a sneer it does not carry on its own.

items.sentence: Mid-rise infill and others of that ___ dominate the pipeline.
Developers of that ___ have ruined three neighbourhoods.

gloss.anachronism: something out of its proper time

sets.why: The error is chronological placement, not age. A working gas lamp is old; a gas lamp in a 1990s film set in 2020 is an anachronism.

items.sentence: The zoning is an ___ — it was written for an industry that left in 1978.
The fax machine in reception is charmingly ___.

gloss.ironic: meaning the opposite of what is said, or an outcome that mocks the intention

sets.why: Irony needs a gap between what was intended and what happened. Bad luck on its own is not ironic, however striking.

items.sentence: It is ___ that the traffic study made the intersection more dangerous.
It was ___ that we both submitted on the same day.

gloss.disabuse: to free someone of a mistaken belief

sets.wrong: to insult, or to stop mistreating
sets.why: Nothing to do with abuse. You disabuse someone of a notion — the notion is what is being removed.

items.sentence: Someone should ___ him of the idea that this is a formality.
The new manager set out to ___ the crew fairly.

sets.why: The son in the parable was prodigal before he left, not because he came back. The word is about spending, not homecoming.

items.sentence: A ___ use of land: three storeys on a site zoned for twelve.
The ___ partner reappeared after four years in Vancouver.

gloss.redundant: surplus to requirements; more than is needed

sets.why: Repetition is one way of being redundant, not the meaning of it. In engineering a redundant member is a deliberate spare, and that is a virtue rather than a fault.

items.sentence: A second stair is ___ in the strict sense and required in every other.
The report is ___, saying the same thing in four places.

gloss.sanction: to authorise and permit — and also to penalise

sets.wrong: only one of the two, whichever you had in mind
sets.why: It is its own opposite. A sanctioned use is a permitted one; sanctions against a country are penalties. Context has to do all the work, so in writing that matters, choose another word.

items.sentence: The use was ___ by the committee in 2019 and has run since.
The regulator will ___ the firm for the late filing.

sets.why: 'We will be landing momentarily' promises a very short landing. Both senses are current, which is exactly why the word is a poor choice when the difference matters.

items.sentence: The power failed ___ and the meeting carried on.
The chair will be with you ___.

gloss.transpire: to become known; to leak out

sets.why: Things transpire the way news does — they emerge. Using it for 'happen' costs you a word that means something else and gains nothing.

items.sentence: It later ___ that the survey had been commissioned by the applicant.
Nothing much ___ at the first meeting.

gloss.careen: to lean over, as a ship does

sets.wrong: to rush headlong — that is career
sets.why: A vehicle that careers down a hill is going fast; one that careens is tipping. They are often doing both, which is how the confusion survives.

items.sentence: The hull ___ as the tide went out under it.
The truck ___ down the ramp and through the hoarding.

gloss.factoid: something that looks like a fact because it has been repeated

sets.why: Norman Mailer coined it for the opposite of a fact. The -oid is the giveaway: humanoid is not a human.

items.sentence: The claim about the 1953 fire is a ___ that has outlived every correction.
The appendix collects a few useful ___ about the watershed.

gloss.complement: to complete, or go well with

sets.why: The one that completes something has the same middle as 'complete'. Everything else is praise.

items.sentence: The new wing ___ the original building rather than competing with it.
She paid him a rare ___ on the drafting.

sets.why: Farther is for distance you could measure. Further is for everything else, including anything you can only measure in degree.

items.sentence: The site is ___ from the station than the plan suggests.
The proposal needs ___ study before it goes to council.

sets.why: Two letters apart and unrelated. Disingenuous — the commoner word — is the negative of the second, not the first.

items.sentence: An ___ solution: the stair doubles as the ventilation shaft.
He gave an ___ answer that gave away rather more than he meant to.

gloss.exacerbate: to make a bad situation worse

sets.why: Situations are exacerbated; people are exasperated.

items.sentence: Widening the road would only ___ the congestion downstream.
Three cancelled meetings in a row ___ the whole committee.

sets.why: You allude to a thing; a thing eludes you. Note also that alluding is indirect — if you named it, you referred to it.

items.sentence: He ___ to the earlier dispute without ever naming it.
The reason for the delay ___ everyone in the room.

sets.why: Three words, one sound. The third is rare enough that using it is a decision; the first two are confused constantly.

items.sentence: An ___ historian was brought in to advise on the restoration.
With a decision ___, both sides stopped negotiating.

gloss.council: a body of people that meets
gloss.counsel: advice, or a lawyer, or to advise

sets.why: A council is a thing you sit on. Counsel is what you give, or who gives it.

items.sentence: The item goes to ___ in November.
She sought ___ before replying to the notice.

sets.why: Envelopes has an e, and so does the stationery you put in them.

items.sentence: Traffic was ___ from the bridge to the underpass.
The letter went out on the firm's ___.

gloss.perquisite: a benefit that comes with a position — a perk

sets.why: A perquisite is a perk, which is the short form of it. A prerequisite is a condition.

items.sentence: A servicing study is a ___ of the application.
The parking space was one of the few ___ of the job.

gloss.practice: the noun — a habit, a profession, a firm
gloss.practise: the verb — to do a thing repeatedly

sets.why: Canadian usage keeps the British split: the noun ends -ice, the verb -ise. Advice and advise settle it — you can hear the difference there.

items.sentence: It is standard ___ to circulate the plans a week ahead.
She has ___ planning in three provinces.

gloss.licence: the noun — the permission or the document

sets.why: Same Canadian rule as practice and practise: -ce for the noun, -se for the verb.

items.sentence: The operator holds a ___ for the patio.
The province ___ the facility for sixty beds.

gloss.envelop: to wrap around (verb, stress on the second syllable)
gloss.envelope: the paper sleeve, or the outer limit of a form

sets.why: One letter, and the stress moves. The building envelope is the noun; fog envelops a site.

items.sentence: Mist would ___ the valley by six most evenings.
The zoning sets the building ___, not the design.

gloss.breach: a break, or to break through

sets.why: A breach of contract is a break in it. Breeches are trousers, and a breech birth comes out backwards.

items.sentence: Building before approval is a clear ___ of the agreement.
The gun was loaded at the ___ rather than the muzzle.

sets.why: The double s is the one you do to people.

items.sentence: The awnings were ___ stretched on a steel frame.
Staff will ___ the neighbourhood before the meeting.

sets.why: Three homophones a planner meets in a single sentence more often than most people.

items.sentence: The report ___ four policies in support of the height.
The ___ slopes away from the street by two metres.

sets.why: Discomfit is about being thrown off, not about being uncomfortable — though the two have run together so far that the distinction is nearly gone.

items.sentence: The question ___ him badly and he lost his thread.
She sat through the hearing in obvious ___.

sets.why: E for exit, i for in. Which one you use depends on where you are standing.

items.sentence: Her grandparents ___ from Portugal in 1963.
They ___ to Canada that same year.

sets.why: Floundering is still going. Foundering is over.

items.sentence: He ___ through the first ten minutes before finding his argument.
The scheme ___ when the financing fell through.

gloss.gambit: an opening move, often a sacrifice

sets.why: You run the gamut and open with a gambit. 'Runs the gambit' is the common error.

items.sentence: The responses ran the ___ from delight to litigation.
Offering the parkland was a ___ to get the height approved.

sets.why: A hoard is treasure. A horde is people. This app is named after the first.

items.sentence: A ___ of Roman coins turned up during the excavation.
A ___ of objectors filled the gallery.

sets.why: The claim is incredible; the listener is incredulous. Only a person can be the second.

items.sentence: The cost estimate was frankly ___.
She listened with an ___ expression and then asked for the figures.

gloss.insidious: harmful in a way that spreads unnoticed
gloss.invidious: likely to cause resentment; unfairly discriminating

sets.why: Insidious damage creeps. An invidious comparison offends.

items.sentence: The rot was ___ — nothing showed until the joists gave.
Ranking the submissions publicly put her in an ___ position.

sets.why: The e makes it a verb, and makes it much stronger. Being loath to do something is mild reluctance, not hatred.

items.sentence: He was ___ to reopen a matter that had taken two years to settle.
She had come to ___ the whole approvals process.

gloss.palate: the roof of the mouth; taste
gloss.pallet: the wooden platform, or a straw bed

sets.why: A material palette is the range of finishes. A pallet is what the bricks arrive on.

items.sentence: The ___ is limited to three materials across the whole facade.
The stone came in on a single ___.

gloss.pique: to provoke or stimulate; also a fit of resentment

sets.why: Interest is piqued, not peaked. A peak in interest is a different claim entirely.

items.sentence: The proposal ___ the committee's interest for the first time.
Demand ___ in 2022 and has fallen since.

gloss.perspective: a point of view; the drawing convention

sets.why: A prospective purchaser is one who might buy. A perspective is how it looks from where you stand.

items.sentence: The ___ tenants were shown the unfinished floor.
From the resident's ___ the loading dock is the whole issue.

sets.why: One describes a place, the other names the people in it.

items.sentence: It is the most ___ ward in the city.
The ___ was never consulted on the alignment.

sets.why: You pore over a document. Pouring over it would ruin it.

items.sentence: They ___ over the survey for most of the afternoon.
The slab was ___ on the Tuesday.

sets.why: Pre- is before. Pro- is forward.

items.sentence: A public meeting must ___ the statutory notice.
The applicant chose to ___ without the variance.

sets.why: People are regretful. Events are regrettable. 'A regretful incident' says the incident had feelings.

items.sentence: The delay was ___ but not anyone's fault.
He sounded genuinely ___ about the way it had been handled.

sets.why: Milton coined the second precisely to escape the first. A sensuous material is one you want to touch; a sensual one is a different review entirely.

items.sentence: The oiled timber gives the room a ___ warmth.
The poem is frankly ___ and was banned for it.

sets.why: A specious argument looks sound and is not. A spurious one is a forgery. The first is the more useful word and the more often missed.

items.sentence: The shadow argument is ___ — it sounds right until you check the angles.
The signature turned out to be ___.

sets.why: You stanch bleeding and have a staunch ally. The spellings have blurred, but the two senses have not.

items.sentence: Nothing they did would ___ the losses.
She was a ___ defender of the heritage designation.

sets.why: Water is turbid. Prose is turgid.

items.sentence: Runoff left the creek ___ for a week afterwards.
Forty pages of ___ prose to say the site is suitable.

sets.why: Waiving a fee gives it up. Waving it through is a different, and vaguer, thing.

items.sentence: Council agreed to ___ the application fee.
He would ___ at the crew from the site office each morning.

sets.why: It whets the appetite — sharpens it. A whetstone is where the word lives.

items.sentence: The preview only ___ their appetite for the full scheme.
He ___ the cloth before wiping the joint.

sets.why: You amend a by-law and emend a manuscript. Emend is only ever about text.

items.sentence: The by-law was ___ to permit the use as of right.
The editor ___ two passages that had been miscopied.

sets.why: One extra c, and it moves from weather to drama.

items.sentence: The design responds to ___ conditions rather than to a style.
The vote was the ___ moment of a two-year process.

sets.why: One is a noun for a person, the other an adjective for a mood.

items.sentence: He had been her ___ since the first year of the partnership.
She was ___ the appeal would not be pursued.

sets.why: The behaviour is contemptible; the look you give it is contemptuous.

items.sentence: Misleading the panel about the survey was ___.
He gave the drawings a ___ glance and pushed them back.

gloss.definitive: conclusive; the final authority on the matter

sets.why: A definite answer is unambiguous. A definitive one settles the question for good, which is a much larger claim.

items.sentence: We need a ___ date before we can book the hall.
The tribunal's ruling is the ___ statement on that provision.

sets.why: Economic development is about the economy. An economical layout wastes less.

items.sentence: The study looks at the ___ impact on the main street.
A single corridor is the more ___ arrangement.

sets.why: An exhaustive review covers everything. An exhausting one merely wore you out.

items.sentence: The list is indicative rather than ___.
Four hours of deputations was ___.

sets.why: A human error is a mistake a person made. A humane decision is a kind one.

items.sentence: The failure was ___ rather than structural.
Rehousing the tenants first was the ___ order to do it in.

sets.why: Lands are industrial. People are industrious.

items.sentence: The block is designated ___ and has been since 1954.
An ___ articling student had indexed every submission.

sets.why: A judicial review happens in a court. A judicious edit shows sense.

items.sentence: The decision is subject to ___ review.
A ___ cut of thirty pages made the report readable.

gloss.disinterested: impartial; having no stake in the outcome

sets.why: The useful sense of disinterested is the one that has no other word. Losing it to 'uninterested' costs the language a term for impartiality and gains nothing.

items.sentence: The dispute needs a ___ chair, someone with nothing to gain either way.
He was so ___ in the report that he never got past the summary.

gloss.fulsome: excessive to the point of insincerity; cloying

sets.why: 'Fulsome praise' is not high praise. It is praise laid on so thick that it curdles. People reach for it as a compliment and deliver an insult.

items.sentence: His ___ tribute to the chair made everyone uncomfortable.
The minutes gave a ___ account of the meeting.

gloss.enervate: to drain of energy; to weaken

sets.why: It looks like it should mean 'put nerve into'. It means the opposite: to take the nerve out.

items.sentence: The heat ___ the crew until nobody could lift anything.
The news ___ the team and they worked through the night.

gloss.nonplussed: so surprised or confused that you cannot react

sets.why: The 'non-' reads like a negation of being bothered. It is not. It is from 'non plus' - the point beyond which you cannot go.

items.sentence: The question left her completely ___; she simply stopped speaking.
He was entirely ___ by the heckling and carried on.

sets.why: Refute claims success. If you only said it was wrong, you rebutted or denied it. Writers use 'refute' to smuggle in a verdict they have not earned.

items.sentence: The soil data ___ the claim outright: there was never any contamination.
She ___ the allegation but offered nothing to support her account.

sets.why: It has been used so often for glancing over something that dictionaries now record both. The careful sense is the older one and the one worth keeping.

items.sentence: She ___ the contract line by line before signing anything.
He ___ the headlines on the way out the door.

sets.why: A fortuitous event may be a disaster. The word carries no luck, only accident - the resemblance to 'fortunate' is doing all the damage.

items.sentence: Their meeting was entirely ___ - neither knew the other would be there.
It was a ___ break that saved the project.

sets.why: You flout a rule and flaunt a possession. 'Flaunting the law' is the commonest version of this error and it reverses the meaning.

items.sentence: The operator ___ the conditions of approval for two years.
He ___ his new title at every opportunity.

sets.why: Militate takes 'against' and pushes; mitigate takes an object and softens. 'Mitigate against' is the error, and it is everywhere.

items.sentence: The cost of servicing ___ against approving the application.
Tree planting would ___ the heat-island effect.

gloss.comprise: to contain; the whole comprises the parts
gloss.compose: to make up; the parts compose the whole

sets.why: The whole comprises the parts - never 'is comprised of'. If you want the passive, the phrase is 'is composed of'.

items.sentence: The site ___ four lots and a laneway.
Four lots and a laneway ___ the site.

sets.why: 'The enormity of the task' says the task is wicked, not large. For size, the word is enormousness or simply scale.

items.sentence: The commission was set up to confront the ___ of what had been done.
Nobody had grasped the sheer ___ of the building.

gloss.restive: restless and hard to control; balky

sets.why: It shares a root with 'rest' and means very nearly the opposite. A restive crowd is on the edge of trouble.

items.sentence: By the third hour the gallery had grown ___ and the chair called a recess.
They spent a ___ weekend by the lake.

sets.why: Nothing to do with noise. It is 'annoy' plus '-some'.

items.sentence: A ___ smell rose off the drain in the summer heat.
The ___ construction started before seven every morning.

sets.why: Conditions are adverse; people are averse. Only a person can be averse, and they are averse *to* something.

items.sentence: The scheme failed under ___ market conditions.
She is not ___ to a long argument.

sets.why: Same origin, split spellings. The one with the two e's separated is the one that means separated.

items.sentence: He made a ___ enquiry before raising it publicly.
The programme runs in three ___ phases.

gloss.prescribe: to lay down as a rule; to order

sets.why: One letter apart and near-opposite. A prescribed use is required; a proscribed one is banned.

items.sentence: The standard ___ a minimum setback of three metres.
The by-law ___ any use that generates odour.

sets.why: Censure is a verdict. Censoring is an act of editing.

items.sentence: Council voted to ___ the member for the remarks.
The broadcaster ___ two minutes of the recording.

gloss.infer: to work out from evidence (the listener)

sets.why: The speaker implies, the listener infers. 'Are you inferring that I lied?' hands your own act to the other person.

items.sentence: Nothing in the letter ___ that the offer was final.
From the silence she ___ that the deal was off.

sets.why: Continual interruptions stop and start. A continuous wall does not.

items.sentence: ___ delays pushed the hearing back three times.
The frontage forms a ___ street wall for the whole block.

gloss.home: to move precisely towards (home in on)

sets.why: You hone a blade or an argument. You home in on a target. 'Honing in' is a blend of the two.

items.sentence: Three drafts later he had ___ the argument to a point.
The review ___ in on a single clause.

sets.why: Appraise sets a value; apprise passes on news.

items.sentence: An agent was hired to ___ the property.
Please ___ the board of the delay.

sets.why: A tortuous route bends. A torturous one hurts. Bureaucracy is usually the first, occasionally both.

items.sentence: The approvals process was long and ___, doubling back on itself.
The last mile in that heat was ___.

sets.why: One letter apart, and it is the difference between a small sin and a bought official.

items.sentence: The inquiry found a ___ official taking payments to expedite files.
A missed footnote is a ___ fault in a document this long.

sets.why: Three words, one root, entirely different jobs. The witness is credible; the audience is credulous; the effort is creditable.

items.sentence: She gave a ___ account that matched the timeline.
A ___ readership will swallow any figure printed in bold.

sets.why: Self-deprecating is disapproval of oneself. Assets depreciate.

items.sentence: He ___ the whole idea in two sentences.
The equipment ___ faster than the schedule assumed.

sets.why: Luxuriant is about growth, not money. Planting is luxuriant; a hotel is luxurious.

items.sentence: The ravine was ___ after a wet spring.
They put the delegates up in ___ rooms.

gloss.simplistic: oversimplified to the point of being wrong

sets.why: It is never neutral and never a compliment. If you mean the explanation was clear, the word is simple.

items.sentence: That reading is ___; it ignores half the evidence.
He gave a ___ explanation that anyone could follow.

sets.why: A substantive objection goes to the merits. A substantial one is merely big.

items.sentence: The response raised no ___ objection to the merits.
A ___ share of the funding came from the province.

sets.why: Systemic describes where a problem lives. Systematic describes how work is done.

items.sentence: The failure was ___, not the fault of any one office.
They made a ___ review of every file from that year.

sets.why: Reticence is about silence. If someone will not do a thing, they are reluctant.

items.sentence: He was ___ about his own part in it and changed the subject.
She was ___ to sign until the survey came back.

sets.why: You defuse a row by taking the fuse out. Diffuse light is scattered.

items.sentence: A short apology ___ the whole argument.
The atrium gives a soft, ___ light all day.

sets.why: Empathy stands inside; sympathy stands beside.

items.sentence: Having lived through the same eviction, she felt real ___ for them.
He sent a note of ___ after the funeral.

gloss.ambivalent: pulled both ways; holding two opposed feelings
gloss.ambiguous: open to more than one reading

sets.why: Ambivalence is a surplus of feeling, not an absence. A person is ambivalent; a sentence is ambiguous.

items.sentence: She was ___ about the move: excited and grieving at once.
The wording is ___ and could be read either way.

gloss.decimate: to destroy a large part of

sets.why: Originally to kill one in ten. The modern sense of heavy loss is now standard - but it still cannot mean total destruction, because something must survive.

items.sentence: Two winters ___ the herd, leaving barely a third alive.
The fire ___ the archive; nothing at all was recovered.

sets.why: It is not an intensifier of 'ultimate'. It is a position, and it is one place before the end.

items.sentence: The argument turns on the ___ paragraph, not the closing one.
This is the ___ authority on the subject.

gloss.meretricious: showily attractive but false or cheap

sets.why: It looks like 'merit' and comes from the Latin for a prostitute. It means the opposite of deserving.

items.sentence: A ___ facade of applied stone over a cheap frame.
The award recognised a long and ___ career.

gloss.beg the question: to assume the very thing you are trying to prove

sets.why: It names a specific fallacy: the conclusion is smuggled into the premise. 'Raises the question' is what people usually mean.

items.sentence: Saying the policy works because it is effective simply ___.
The overrun ___ whether the estimate was ever realistic.

sets.why: The extra e sends it forward in time, not away. 'The foregoing paragraph' is the one above; to forgo a fee is to waive it.

items.sentence: They agreed to ___ the escalation clause.
Nothing in the ___ analysis contradicts that.

gloss.principal: chief; or the head of a firm; or a capital sum

sets.why: Principle is only ever a noun and only ever a rule. Everything else is principal.

items.sentence: The ___ objection is one of scale, not use.
She refused on ___ and would not be moved.

sets.why: One is a verb, one is an adjective, and they sound identical.

items.sentence: The survey failed to ___ a single useful response.
The unit was being run as an ___ short-term rental.

sets.why: Wreak is almost always followed by havoc. The past tense is wreaked, not wrought.

items.sentence: The storm ___ havoc on the temporary works.
One bad decision ___ the whole schedule.

sets.why: Nothing fazes her. The work proceeds in phases.

items.sentence: The hostile room did not ___ him at all.
The second ___ starts in the spring.

gloss.tenet: a principle held to be true

sets.why: A central tenet is a belief. A tenant pays rent.

items.sentence: The central ___ of the approach is that density follows transit.
Every ___ in the building received notice.

sets.why: A historic decision changes things. A historical record merely dates from then.

items.sentence: The vote was a ___ turning point for the city.
The claim rests on ___ evidence from the 1890s.

sets.why: Fewer units, less floor area. The exception is measures treated as a single amount: less than five years.

items.sentence: The revision proposes ___ units on the same footprint.
The revision proposes ___ floor area overall.

sets.why: You assure a person, ensure an outcome, insure a building.
